# Philosophical and Technological Thinkers:
This section profiles diverse innovators in computing and science, ranging from early pioneers like Charles Babbage (Difference and Analytical Engines) and Ada Lovelace (foreseeing general-purpose computation) to modern figures. Key contributors include Alfred North Whitehead (process ontology), Leonardo Torres Quevedo (Telekino), Alan Turing (Turing machine/Test), Blaise Pascal (Pascaline), and the inventors of frequency-hopping spread spectrum (Hedy Lamarr and George Antheil). Vannevar Bush coordinated WWII science and proposed the "memex," while Claude Shannon's digital circuit theory was advanced by Bush's MIT students. Philip Rubin is a prominent interdisciplinary researcher in embodied cognition, known for developing foundational speech technology models (ASY, SWS) and advancing speech theory using dynamical systems. Beyond his technical achievements, Rubin is a significant policy influencer, holding roles such as director of the NSF's Division of Behavioral and Cognitive Sciences and advisor to the White House OSTP on neuroscience, alongside leadership positions at UConn and Haskins Laboratories, and serving on various advisory boards. His research spans speech and perception (including phoneme detection and speech production theory), motor control (human interlimb coordination), and research ethics and policy, often collaborating with researchers like Remez and Goldstein. Rubin's work has also appeared in popular culture, such as in a 2022 illustration by Drew Friedman in *Mineshaft* .

# Software Freedom Advocacy and Activism:
Richard Stallman is a leading advocate for free software, founder of the Free Software Foundation (FSF) in 1985, and driving force behind the GNU project. He champions copyleft via the GPL (creating tools like GNU Emacs and GCC) and opposes proprietary restrictions, maintaining roles as a MacArthur Fellow and anti-surveillance activist.
